beginner: Potatoes want loose, well-drained soil that the growing tubers can swell into easily. Light, sandy or loamy soil with plenty of compost works best. Heavy, soggy clay is the main thing to avoid: it holds water and rots the seed pieces and tubers, and it makes the potatoes come out knobby. If your soil is heavy clay, a raised bed or a deep container of loose mix is the easy fix. Keep the soil on the acidic side (pH about 5.0 to 6.0), which also helps prevent scab, the rough corky patches on the skin. Do not add fresh manure, because it makes scab worse.
seasoned: Potatoes need loose, friable, well-drained soil so the developing tubers can expand without resistance and the seed pieces do not rot. A light sandy loam or loam worked deep and amended with compost gives the best yields and the cleanest skin; cold, wet, heavy clay rots seed pieces, restricts tuber growth, and produces knobby, misshapen potatoes, and is best improved with organic matter or replaced with a raised bed. Keep the soil acidic, roughly pH 5.0 to 6.0, which suppresses common scab. Avoid fresh manure and excess nitrogen: manure encourages scab, and too much nitrogen drives leafy top growth at the expense of tubers. Steady, even moisture in well-drained soil is the goal, never waterlogged ground.

beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Potatoes like it on the acidic side, about 5.0 to 6.0, which is lower (more acidic) than most vegetables. There is a good reason: keeping the soil acidic helps prevent scab, the rough corky patches that form on the potato skin. Scab gets worse when the soil is less acidic and dry, so if scab is a problem, aim toward the low end (around 5.0 to 5.3) and keep the soil evenly moist while the tubers are forming. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number.
seasoned: Potatoes grow best in acidic soil, roughly pH 5.0 to 6.0, lower than most garden vegetables. The acidity is deliberate disease management: common scab (Streptomyces scabies) is suppressed in acidic soil and worsens as pH rises above about 5.5, especially in dry soil. Where scab is a recurring problem, hold the pH between about 5.0 and 5.3 and keep the soil evenly moist for the 4 to 9 weeks after planting when tubers are forming. Potatoes tolerate a wider band (down to about 4.8 and up to 6.5), and they will grow at neutral pH, but scab pressure climbs with pH, so do not lime a potato bed. A soil test removes the guesswork before planting.

beginner: Potatoes need a moderate amount of food. Mix a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 into the row when you plant, then feed lightly again about a month later as the plants grow. Do not pile on high-nitrogen fertilizer or fresh manure: too much nitrogen grows big leafy tops but fewer potatoes, and manure makes scab worse. Compost mixed into the bed is the safe way to enrich the soil.
seasoned: Potatoes are moderate feeders. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the row at planting (UGA suggests about 1.5 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress lightly about 4 weeks later as the tops fill in and again as the vines spread. Favor balanced feeding over heavy nitrogen: excess nitrogen grows lush vines and delays tuber formation, and fresh manure encourages scab, so use only well-finished compost. Adequate potassium supports tuber quality.

beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Potatoes do best with a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10, not a high-nitrogen one. Too much of the first number grows leaves instead of potatoes, and fresh manure brings on scab, so use compost and a balanced feed.
seasoned: Potatoes are moderate feeders that want balanced nutrition with good potassium and only modest nitrogen. A balanced blend such as 10-10-10 worked into the row at planting covers most home soils. Too much nitrogen drives vines instead of tubers, and fresh manure encourages scab, so lean on compost and a balanced fertilizer rather than a high-nitrogen feed.

beginner: Mix in about 1.5 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet when you plant, then feed lightly again about a month later. Go easy: more fertilizer does not mean more potatoes, and too much nitrogen just grows leaves.
seasoned: Work about 1.5 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet into the row at planting (UGA), and side-dress a similar light amount about 4 weeks later and again as the vines spread. Keep nitrogen modest; excess nitrogen delays tuberization and grows vines at the expense of tubers.

beginner: Potatoes are easygoing with most neighbors. Beans and peas are a classic match because they add nitrogen to the soil, and bush beans are said to help keep the Colorado potato beetle down. The plants to keep well away are potato's nightshade relatives, tomato, pepper, and eggplant, because they share the same diseases, especially late blight, and the same soil pests. Do not trust every companion chart online; many of their claims have never been tested.
seasoned: Potatoes mix easily into the garden. The best-grounded pairings are with legumes (beans, peas), which fix nitrogen and are traditionally credited with deterring the Colorado potato beetle. The clearest avoids are potato's own family, the nightshades: tomato, pepper, and eggplant share late blight and other soilborne diseases and pests, so keep them apart and rotate among them on a multi-year cycle. Most other companion-chart claims for potato are folklore; treat them with healthy skepticism, since university reviews find little evidence behind most of them.

beginner: Beans are legumes that pull nitrogen from the air and leave some in the soil, and many gardeners plant bush beans near potatoes to help fend off the Colorado potato beetle. It is a popular, sensible pairing, though the pest-deterrent part is traditional rather than proven.
seasoned: Beans and potatoes are a classic reciprocal pairing. As legumes, beans fix nitrogen and undemanding bush beans share a bed without competing hard, and tradition holds that beans deter Colorado potato beetle while potatoes deter Mexican bean beetle. The nitrogen contribution is real; treat the mutual pest-repellence as traditional rather than proven.

beginner: Leafy brassicas like cabbage, kale, and lettuce-style greens grow in the same cool season as potatoes and use the bed without fighting for the same below-ground space, a handy way to fit more into a spring garden.
seasoned: Cool-season leafy crops (cabbage-family greens, lettuce) overlap potato's spring window and root shallowly, so they share the bed efficiently while the potato builds tubers below. This is a space-and-timing interplant, not a measured pest benefit, but it is a reliable way to use a spring bed.

beginner: An old tradition is to plant horseradish at the corner of the potato patch, where some gardeners believe it helps keep the potatoes healthier. It spreads aggressively, so keep it contained or in its own spot.
seasoned: Planting horseradish at the edge of the potato patch is traditional lore said to improve potato health. There is no controlled evidence for it, and horseradish spreads aggressively, so contain it. Recorded for growers who keep the tradition, not as a proven tactic.

beginner: Tomatoes are potato's close cousin (both nightshades) and catch the same diseases, especially late blight, which can wipe out both. Keep them well apart, and do not plant potatoes where tomatoes, peppers, or eggplant grew last year.
seasoned: Tomatoes and potatoes are both Solanaceae and share their worst diseases, including late blight (Phytophthora infestans) and early blight, plus soilborne pests. Grown together they form a disease bridge that can destroy both crops, so keep them apart and rotate so potatoes never follow tomato, pepper, or eggplant.

beginner: Peppers and eggplant are also nightshades, like potatoes, so they share the same soil diseases and pests. Grow them in a different part of the garden and rotate where each goes each year.
seasoned: Peppers and eggplant are nightshade relatives that share potato's soilborne diseases (Verticillium, early blight) and pests (flea beetles). Clustering the family or following one with another sustains that pressure, which is why extension guidance rotates potatoes well away from all Solanaceae.

beginner: Leaves chewed ragged, sometimes stripped to the stems. The beetles are oval, about 3/8 inch, with yellow and black stripes; the larvae are fat, pinkish-orange grubs with black heads; and the eggs are clusters of bright orange ovals on the undersides of leaves. The big grubs do most of the eating, and damage hurts most once the potatoes are forming underneath.
seasoned: Ragged, chewed foliage that can be stripped to the stems in a bad outbreak. Look for oval, 3/8-inch adults with yellow and black lengthwise stripes, plump pink-to-salmon larvae with black heads and two rows of dark spots, and bright yellowish-orange egg clusters on the undersides of leaves. The last-stage larvae do most of the damage. Potatoes tolerate up to about 30 percent defoliation before flowering but only about 10 percent once tubers are sizing.

beginner: The Colorado potato beetle, a striped beetle that spends winter in the soil near old potato patches and comes out in spring to feed and lay eggs. Each female lays hundreds of eggs and there can be two rounds in a summer, so numbers build fast. It also goes after eggplant and other nightshades.
seasoned: Larvae and adults of the Colorado potato beetle (Leptinotarsa decemlineata), which overwinter 5 to 10 inches deep in soil in and around last year's potatoes and emerge in spring to feed and lay eggs. Each female lays up to 350 eggs, and there is often a second generation by midsummer in central and southern areas. It also attacks eggplant and other nightshades.

beginner: Pick the beetles, grubs, and orange egg clusters off by hand and drop them in soapy water; check the plants every couple of days. There is no easy spray fix, because the beetles have grown resistant to many of them, so hand-removal is the most reliable home control.
seasoned: Handpicking is effective in a home garden: knock adults and larvae into a pail of soapy water and crush the orange egg clusters on the leaf undersides; check every few days. There is no quick spray cure, and the beetle has developed resistance to many insecticides, so persistence with handpicking and removal does most of the work.

beginner: Move potatoes to a new spot each year, away from where they (or eggplant) grew last year, because the beetles wake up right there in spring. A row cover over the bed early keeps them off, straw mulch slows them down, and crushing the first egg clusters stops a generation before it starts.
seasoned: Rotate potatoes well away from last year's bed, since the overwintered adults emerge where potatoes grew before. Floating row cover laid over the bed at emergence keeps the beetles off until you need to remove it for the developing plants, and a thick straw mulch can slow the adults walking in. Crush early egg clusters before they hatch to break the first generation.

beginner: Lots of tiny holes in the leaves, as if peppered with shot, made by little dark beetles that hop away when you come near. Young plants are hurt most; big healthy plants shrug it off. The grubs can also nibble the tubers.
seasoned: Tiny dark beetles that jump when disturbed and chew many small round shot-holes in the leaves. Heavy early feeding on young plants stunts growth; the larvae feed on roots and can leave small tracks or pits on tubers. Established, vigorous plants usually outgrow light feeding.

beginner: Small beetles called flea beetles that spend winter nearby and jump onto young potato plants in spring. They do the most harm to little plants and in warm, dry spells.
seasoned: Several species of small flea beetles, including the tuber flea beetle, that overwinter nearby and move onto young potato foliage in spring. They are worst on small, slow plants and in warm, dry weather.

beginner: Keep young plants growing strong with steady water and they usually outgrow the damage. A row cover protects seedlings early on, and clearing weeds and old plant debris takes away their winter hiding spots.
seasoned: Healthy, well-watered plants usually outgrow flea beetle damage. Floating row cover protects young plants during the vulnerable early weeks; remove it once the plants are established. Clearing weeds and old crop debris reduces the shelter they overwinter in.

beginner: Move the potatoes to a new spot, pull weeds, and cover the young plants until they are big and strong. Plants that are well fed and watered handle flea beetles much better than struggling ones.
seasoned: Rotate away from last year's nightshade beds, keep the area weed-free, and protect young plants with row cover until they are large enough to tolerate feeding. Vigorous, evenly watered plants are far more tolerant than stressed ones.

beginner: Tiny soft insects, usually green or pink, crowded on the new growth and the undersides of leaves, sometimes leaving a sticky film. Their feeding is minor, but they can pass on plant viruses that make the leaves mottle, curl, or roll and cut your harvest. A plant that catches a virus will not get better.
seasoned: Small soft-bodied insects, often green or pink, clustered on growing tips and leaf undersides, sometimes with sticky honeydew and sooty mold. The bigger problem is not their feeding but the viruses they transmit (such as potato virus Y and leafroll), which cause mottled, curled, or rolled leaves and reduce yield; virus-infected plants do not recover.

beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects, and as they move from plant to plant they carry potato viruses. The viruses, more than the bugs, are the real concern, which is why it is best to plant certified disease-free seed potatoes instead of saving your own.
seasoned: Several aphid species colonize potato foliage, and as they move plant to plant they spread potato viruses. Virus pressure, not the feeding itself, is the main reason to manage them, and it is the reason gardeners are advised to start from certified disease-free seed potatoes rather than saved tubers.

beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes so the patch starts clean. A little aphid activity is fine, because ladybugs and other helpers usually keep them in check; for heavy clusters, spray them off with water or use insecticidal soap. Pull and throw away any plant that clearly has a virus.
seasoned: Start with certified seed potatoes to keep virus out of the patch. Tolerate light aphid numbers, since beneficial insects (ladybugs, lacewings, parasitic wasps) often control them; a strong spray of water or insecticidal soap knocks down heavy colonies. Remove and destroy any plant showing clear virus symptoms.

beginner: Buy certified seed potatoes, avoid harsh sprays that kill the helpful bugs, keep weeds down, and pull out any virus-looking plant right away so it does not spread.
seasoned: Use certified seed potatoes, encourage beneficial insects by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays, control nearby weeds that host aphids and virus, and rogue out virus-symptomatic plants promptly so they do not seed an outbreak.

beginner: Hard, shiny, tan-colored worms in the soil that drill narrow holes into the potatoes. You usually do not notice anything above ground; you find the little tunnels when you dig the crop. Tunneled potatoes do not store well.
seasoned: Slender, shiny, yellow-brown, hard-bodied larvae in the soil that bore narrow holes straight into the tubers, leaving clean round tunnels that downgrade quality and invite rot in storage. There are no useful aboveground symptoms; the damage is found at harvest.

beginner: The larvae of click beetles. They live in the soil for years and are most common in beds that were lawn or grass not long ago. You tend to find them only when you dig.
seasoned: The larvae of click beetles, which live in the soil for several years and are most common in ground recently in sod or grass. They feed on many roots and tubers and are hard to detect until harvest.

beginner: You cannot fix potatoes that are already tunneled, so cut out the bad parts and eat those first instead of storing them. Dig the crop on time rather than leaving it in the ground, where the worms keep boring.
seasoned: There is no rescue for tunneled tubers; trim damaged areas and use them first rather than storing them. Harvest promptly once the crop matures rather than leaving tubers in infested soil, where damage accumulates.

beginner: Do not plant potatoes in a bed that was grass or lawn in the last year or two, where wireworms are worst. Rotate your crops, work the soil, and dig on time. If wireworms keep ruining a bed, use a raised bed with clean soil.
seasoned: Avoid planting potatoes in ground that was recently lawn or pasture, since wireworm numbers are highest there. Rotate, keep the soil well worked, and harvest on time. Where wireworm history is bad, grow elsewhere or in clean raised-bed soil.

beginner: Dark, wet-looking spots on the leaves and stems that spread fast, with a fuzzy white mold underneath in cool, damp weather. The plants can collapse in just a few days, and the rot moves down into the potatoes, leaving firm reddish-brown corky patches inside. This is the famous, most dangerous potato disease, the one behind the Irish famine.
seasoned: Dark, water-soaked spots that appear on leaves and stems and enlarge rapidly, often with a downy white mold on the leaf undersides in cool, wet weather. The foliage can collapse within days, and the disease moves into the tubers, which develop a firm, reddish-brown, dry, corky rot beneath the skin. This is the disease behind the Irish potato famine and the most serious threat to a potato crop.

beginner: A fungus-like organism (Phytophthora infestans) that thrives in cool, wet, humid weather and blows in on the wind. It attacks tomatoes too, so an infected tomato nearby is a danger, and it survives in leftover infected potatoes.
seasoned: The water mold Phytophthora infestans, favored by cool, wet, humid weather and spread on wind and splashing water. It infects both potato and tomato, so a nearby infected tomato is a real risk, and it survives between seasons in infected tubers and cull piles.

beginner: You cannot cure a badly infected plant, so pull and destroy infected plants fast (do not compost them) to slow it down. In a wet year a copper fungicide started early can help, but mostly it is about prevention. Throw away every infected potato so it does not bring the disease back next year.
seasoned: There is no home cure once a plant is badly infected. Remove and destroy infected plants quickly to slow spread, and do not compost them. In wet seasons a copper-based fungicide applied early and repeated can suppress it, but the real defenses are cultural. Destroy all infected tubers so they cannot carry it over.

beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes and a resistant variety like Kennebec, water at the soil in the morning so the leaves stay dry, give plants room for air to move, and keep them away from tomatoes. Clean up any leftover or volunteer potatoes, and cut and remove infected vines before you dig so the disease does not reach the potatoes.
seasoned: Start with certified disease-free seed, choose resistant varieties (such as Kennebec or Sebago), keep foliage dry by watering at the base in the morning, space for airflow, and never plant near tomatoes. Remove volunteer potatoes and cull piles that harbor the pathogen, and destroy any infected vines before harvest so spores do not reach the tubers.

beginner: Dark spots with rings inside them, like a little target or bull's-eye, on the older lower leaves, often with a yellow edge. The spots spread and the lower leaves die off; in a bad case the plant loses its leaves and the potatoes get brown corky patches. Tired, stressed plants get it worst.
seasoned: Small dark brown to black lesions on the older, lower leaves, each with concentric rings that give a target or bull's-eye look, often ringed by a yellow halo. Spots multiply and merge and the lower canopy dies back; severe infection causes defoliation and brown, corky, dry spots on the tubers. Stressed and aging plants are hit hardest.

beginner: A fungus (Alternaria solani) that lives on old plant debris and in the soil and spreads in warm, damp weather. It comes on gradually, especially on stressed plants, rather than wiping a plant out overnight like late blight.
seasoned: The fungus Alternaria solani, which survives on crop debris and in the soil and spreads in warm, humid weather with wet foliage. It is more of a slow, stress-related decline than the explosive collapse of late blight.

beginner: Pick off the worst spotted lower leaves, keep the plants healthy with even water and feeding, and water at the soil so the leaves dry fast. A copper fungicide can help if you start early in a wet spell, but keeping plants strong and the leaves dry does most of the work.
seasoned: Remove badly spotted lower leaves, keep plants vigorous with steady water and feeding (stress worsens it), and water at the base in the morning. A copper or other labeled fungicide can slow spread in a wet season if started early, but cultural care carries most of the load.

beginner: Do not grow potatoes (or tomatoes and peppers) in the same spot for a few years, use clean seed and a resistant variety, clear away old plant debris, give plants room, water at the base, and keep them well fed so they stay strong.
seasoned: Rotate potatoes and other nightshades out of the bed for several years, start with clean seed and resistant varieties, clear crop debris, space and hill for airflow, avoid overhead watering, and keep plants well nourished so they resist the slow decline.

beginner: Rough, brown, corky patches or pits on the potato skin, sometimes spreading into larger areas. The leaves look fine, so you only see it when you dig the potatoes. It does not rot them, it just roughens the skin, and they are fine to eat once peeled, but they do not store or sell as well.
seasoned: Rough, brown, corky scabs or pits on the tuber skin that can merge into larger patches; sometimes raised, sometimes sunken. The leaves and stems are not affected, so it is found only at harvest. It is a skin-quality problem rather than a rot, and the potatoes are fine to eat after peeling, but it downgrades appearance and storage.

beginner: A soil germ (Streptomyces scabies) that gets worse when the soil is not acidic enough (above about pH 5.5), when it is dry while the potatoes are forming, and when fresh manure is used. It lives in the soil for years, so just rotating crops does not get rid of it.
seasoned: The soil bacterium Streptomyces scabies, which is favored by less-acidic soil (pH above about 5.5), dry conditions while tubers are forming, and fresh manure. It persists for years in the soil and on many hosts, so rotation alone does not eliminate it.

beginner: You cannot fix scabbed potatoes, but they are fine to eat after peeling. There is no spray for it; you prevent it by managing the soil instead.
seasoned: There is no rescue once tubers are scabbed; the potatoes are still edible after peeling. Management is preventive: it is controlled by soil conditions, not a spray.

beginner: Keep the soil acidic (about pH 5.0 to 5.3 if scab is a problem) and never add lime to a potato bed. Keep the soil evenly moist while the potatoes are forming, skip fresh manure, plant a scab-resistant variety if it keeps happening, and rotate the bed every few years.
seasoned: Keep soil acidic, around pH 5.0 to 5.3 where scab is a problem, and never lime a potato bed. Keep the soil evenly moist for the 4 to 9 weeks after planting when tubers form, avoid fresh manure, and grow scab-resistant varieties (such as Russet Burbank or Superior) where the disease recurs. Rotate on a 3 to 4 year cycle.

beginner: Blackleg makes the bottom of the stem turn black and slimy while the top of the plant yellows, wilts, and stays small, usually from a bad seed piece. Soft rot turns the potatoes themselves into a soft, wet, smelly mush, in the ground or in storage. Both get into the potato through cuts and bruises and spread in wet conditions.
seasoned: Blackleg shows as an inky-black, slimy rot at the base of the stem with yellowed, wilting, stunted tops, often from infected seed; bacterial soft rot turns tubers into a soft, wet, foul-smelling mush, in the ground or in storage, and can rot a tuber completely within days. The bacteria enter through wounds and spread in wet conditions.

beginner: Bacteria that thrive in wet, poorly drained, warm soil and spread through cuts. They often come in on a bad seed piece, and they are worst when the soil is waterlogged or when bruised potatoes are stored damp.
seasoned: Bacteria in the Pectobacterium and related groups, which are favored by wet soil, poor drainage, and warm conditions, and which spread on cutting knives and through wounds. They often arrive on infected or poorly cured seed pieces and are worst in waterlogged ground and in bruised, wet-stored tubers.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant or potato is infected, so pull out affected plants and never store soft or damaged potatoes. The fix is prevention: be gentle with the tubers and keep them dry.
seasoned: There is no cure for an infected plant or tuber; remove and discard affected plants and do not store blemished or soft potatoes. Management is preventive: handle tubers gently and keep them dry.

beginner: Use certified, well-cured seed pieces and plant them in warm, well-drained soil, not cold mud. Let cut seed pieces heal before planting, do not overwater, dig in dry weather, and handle the potatoes gently. Never store bruised or wet potatoes.
seasoned: Plant certified, well-cured seed pieces (or whole small seed potatoes) in warm, well-drained soil, let cut seed suberize before planting, avoid overwatering and waterlogged beds, harvest in dry conditions, cure the crop, and avoid bruising. Do not store damaged or wet tubers.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, especially once the plants flower and the potatoes start forming underneath. Give about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings. Steady water makes smooth potatoes; letting the soil go dry and then soaking it makes them knobby and cracked and brings on more scab.
seasoned: Potatoes want steady, even moisture, especially from the time tubers begin forming (around flowering) through bulking. Aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings. Even moisture is what produces smooth, well-shaped tubers; a dry-then-wet swing causes knobby growth, growth cracks, and hollow heart, and it worsens scab.

beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, and a bit more in hot or sandy conditions. Do not let the bed dry out while the potatoes are sizing up. Ease off on water once the tops start to yellow and die back, so the skins toughen before you dig.
seasoned: About 1 inch per week including rainfall, increased in heat or sandy soil. The critical window is from tuber initiation through bulking; do not let the bed dry out then. Taper off as the vines yellow and die so the crop can cure and the skins set before harvest.

beginner: Water at the soil with a soaker hose or drip line instead of overhead, because wet leaves bring on blight. A layer of mulch helps keep the moisture steady and the soil cooler around the potatoes.
seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line to keep foliage dry, since wet leaves favor late and early blight. Mulch helps hold even moisture and keeps the soil cooler over the developing tubers.

beginner: If the soil stays soaking wet, the seed pieces and potatoes rot. Watch for yellowing, wilting from the bottom, a sour-smelling soggy bed, and soft potatoes; if you see these, water less and fix the drainage.
seasoned: Constantly saturated soil rots seed pieces and tubers and drives soft rot and blackleg; yellowing, wilting from the base, a sour waterlogged bed, and soft tubers are signs to back off and improve drainage.

beginner: Droopy leaves in the afternoon, dull color, and slow growth mean the plants are thirsty. The bigger problem is letting the soil go dry and then flooding it while the potatoes are sizing, which makes them knobby and cracked.
seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day, dull foliage, and slow growth signal too little water; the sharper risk is an irregular dry-then-soaked cycle during tuber sizing, which causes knobs, growth cracks, and hollow heart.

beginner: While the potatoes are sprouting, keep the soil just evenly damp, not soggy. Too much water now rots the seed pieces before they get going.
seasoned: While the seed pieces sprout and push up, keep the bed evenly moist but not wet: waterlogged soil rots the seed pieces before they establish.

beginner: As the plants grow, water deeply at the base, about an inch a week, and keep the leaves dry to avoid blight. Mulch helps keep the moisture steady and the soil cool.
seasoned: As the tops grow, water deeply at the base, about an inch a week, keeping the foliage dry against early and late blight. Mulch holds even moisture and keeps the soil cooler over the developing tubers.

beginner: Once the plants flower and the potatoes start forming underneath, keep the soil evenly moist. This is when even watering decides how many potatoes you get and helps prevent scab.
seasoned: From about flowering, as tubers begin to form, the make-or-break window opens: even moisture now sets tuber number and helps limit scab. Do not let the bed dry out.

beginner: While the potatoes are sizing up, keep the water steady. Letting the soil go dry and then soaking it makes them knobby, cracked, and hollow inside, and brings on more scab, so even moisture is the key to smooth potatoes.
seasoned: Tuber bulking is the peak: even moisture produces smooth, well-shaped potatoes, while a dry-then-wet swing here drives knobby growth, growth cracks, and hollow heart, and it worsens scab. Keep it steady, more in heat or sandy soil, and never waterlog the bed.

beginner: As the tops start to yellow and die down, ease off the water. That dry finish toughens the skins so the potatoes store well.
seasoned: Ease off water as the vines yellow and die back so the crop can cure and the skins set before digging; a dry finish toughens the skins for storage.

beginner: Water at the soil, not over the leaves, and keep it steady. Wet leaves bring disease, and on-again off-again watering while the potatoes form makes them lumpy and cracked, so even moisture and a little mulch help a lot.
seasoned: Keep water off the foliage and even at the root zone. Wet leaves favor blight, while uneven soil moisture during tuber formation drives knobby, cracked, and hollow tubers, so steady base watering plus mulch is the goal.

seasoned: The make-or-break window is tuber initiation through bulking, from about flowering onward: even moisture here sets tuber number, size, and shape and limits scab. Ease watering as the vines die back so skins set for storage.

beginner: You do not harden off potatoes. They are grown from seed pieces planted straight into the ground, not from indoor-raised seedlings, so there is no transplant step.

Grow potatoes from seed potatoes, which are small whole potatoes or cut pieces, bought as certified disease-free stock (not from the grocery store, and not from packets of seed). Cut bigger ones into chunky pieces about the size of an egg, each with one or two eyes (the little dimples that sprout), and let the cut sides dry and heal for a few days before planting. Plant the pieces cut-side down about 3 to 5 inches deep, 10 to 12 inches apart, in rows about 3 feet apart, once the soil has warmed to about 50°F. There is nothing to start indoors and nothing to harden off.
seasoned: Plant potatoes from certified seed potatoes, not grocery-store tubers (which may carry disease or be sprout-inhibited) and not true seed. Cut larger seed potatoes into blocky pieces of about 1.5 to 2 ounces, each with at least one or two eyes, and let the cut surfaces heal (suberize) for a few days in a warm, humid spot before planting; small egg-sized tubers can be planted whole. Plant pieces cut-side down about 3 to 5 inches deep in rows 30 to 36 inches apart, spacing the pieces 10 to 12 inches apart, once the soil reaches about 50°F. There is no indoor-start or hardening-off step.

beginner: Use a deep, roomy container so you can mound soil up over the plants as they grow. A grow bag or tub of at least 10 gallons (bigger is better) and at least 14 inches deep works well. Start with soil partway up and add more as the plants get taller. Fabric grow bags are easy and drain well.
seasoned: Depth and volume matter more than width: the container must give room to hill soil over the developing tubers. Use a grow bag or tub of at least 10 gallons (15 or more is better) and at least 14 inches deep, filling it part way at planting and adding soil as the plants grow. beginner: Potatoes are a cool-weather crop grown for the starchy tubers that form underground. You do not grow them from seed: you plant seed potatoes, which are small whole potatoes or cut chunks, each with an eye or two, set right in the soil. The leafy tops are tender and killed by hard frost, so in cold places potatoes are a spring crop, and in warm places they are grown through fall and winter. The key trick is hilling: as the plants grow, you mound soil up over the row. This gives the potatoes room to form and, most importantly, keeps them covered so they do not turn green, because green potatoes are bitter and mildly poisonous. Potatoes grow best in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and they like cool soil to make tubers, so heat slows them down. They are ready when the tops turn yellow and die back, about 3 to 4 months after planting, and you can dig a few small new potatoes a bit earlier. Keep potatoes away from their cousins (tomatoes, peppers, eggplant), which share the same diseases, especially late blight, the famous one behind the Irish potato famine.
seasoned: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is a cool-season member of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) grown for its starchy underground tubers. It is planted not from seed but from seed potatoes: small whole tubers or cut pieces, each carrying one or more eyes, set directly in the ground. The foliage is frost tender, so the tops are killed by hard frost even though the crop is grown in the cool season; in cold climates it is a single spring crop, and in mild and hot climates a fall-through-winter crop. The signature practice is hilling: soil is mounded over the row as the plants grow, which expands the zone where tubers form and, critically, keeps them covered and out of the light, since exposed tubers turn green and develop bitter, mildly toxic solanine. Tubers set and bulk best in cool soil, roughly 60 to 70°F, and tuber formation falls off in sustained heat. The crop is ready when the tops yellow and die back, about 90 to 120 days from planting, with thin-skinned new potatoes dug a few weeks earlier. Potatoes prefer loose, well-drained, acidic soil (pH about 5.0 to 6.0, lower than most vegetables) which suppresses common scab, and they are rotated away from their nightshade relatives (tomato, pepper, eggplant) to limit shared disease, above all late blight, the water mold behind the historic Irish potato famine.
